newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks close down but off lows.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks close down but off lows.

text.p: Mexican stocks closed down on Tuesday after a cautious and nervous session kept buyers away, but were still off lows.
"The bourse was nervous and discouraged when the peso was hit by speculation and by forecasts of primary interest rate hikes," said Hans Klingbeil, trader with the Goldman Sachs brokerage in Mexico.
"Bargain hunters stepped in towards the close as stocks had been hit very hard," he added.
The blue chip index closed down 17.99 points, or 0.54 percent, at 3,199.08.

A Reuters survey of 10 money market traders showed they expected bellwether 28-day Cetes to rise by an average of 141 basis points, to 29.11 percent, at the primary Cetes auction, whose results were due Tuesday evening.
The benchmark 48-hour peso meanwhile closed 3.6 centavos weaker at 7.9350/7.9400 per dollar.

Analysts said investor interest also flagged for technical reasons and uncertainty over official economic policy criteria for 1997. "Jitters appeared when the 3,200 point support was broken," said Jaime Fernndez, analyst at the Interacciones brokerage.

"Then some panic selling began, but few wanted to buy either, and that can be seen by the thin volume we had," Fernndez added. Volume was 83.8 million shares traded, but that was inflated by cross trades in Moderna and Kimber.

"The Alliance for Economic Growth cleared up some doubts, but the outlook needs to be completed by official 1997 economic policy criteria, which is what investors are waiting for," said Roberto Galvn, analyst at the Bursamtrica consultancy.
On the broad market scoreboard, a total of 104 stocks were traded, of which losers outnumbered gainers by 62 to 26.

Financial stock GFInver led the gainers list, in what traders said was a technical rebound after it had been hit severely in the wake of a takeover annoucement by Banco Santander last week. The stock had gained on rumors of a takeover, but fell once the actual details were released.
Debt-ridden holding company Sidek led the losers, closely followed by its sister companies, steelmakers Simec and tourist operator Situr.
Traders said the three were hit by Sidek posting net nine month losses on Monday, and by a judge ruling against the firm in a lawsuit the same day.
